title: Ex Oriente Odysseus: the Babylonian Connection of a Greek Hero
author: Jacques R. Pauwels
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/telemachusslaughter-680x537.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/21/ex-
oriente-odysseus-the-babylonian-connection-of-a-greek-hero/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/pauwels1.png)

Odysseus, the Navigator.

> Happy is he who, like Odysseus, made a beautiful journey, (…)  
>  And then returned, full of experience and wisdom  
>  To live among his relatives for the rest of his life!
>
> _– French Renaissance poet Joachim du Bellay (1522-1560)[[1]]()_

The Odyssey is a Greek epic poem describing the decade-long peregrinations of
one of the Greek heroes of the Trojan War, Odysseus, on his way back to his
home on the island of Ithaca. Its twin opus is the Iliad, which focuses on the
story of that war, a conflict involving the siege and eventual destruction by
the Greeks of Troy, a city in northwestern Anatolia, whose location allowed it
to control passage through the Dardanelles, the strategically and commercially
important strait connecting the Aegean Sea, and the entire Mediterranean, to
the Black Sea; Troy was also known as Ilion (or Ilium), hence the title
_Iliad,_ meaning “Saga of Troy.”

The Iliad and the Odyssey were long believed to have been the creation of a
sole ancient Greek author named Homer; however, in the late 19th century
historians became increasingly convinced that those two epic poems were likely
the work of different authors who, sometime between 800 and 700 BCE, put into
writing what had been orally transmitted stories inspired by a historic war
that had been fought much earlier, namely around 1,200 BCE, that is, at the
end of the Bronze Age. A poet named Homer, then, might never have existed:
Homer was almost certainly a “composite character” or “personification” of the
multiple anonymous poets and singers who created and popularized the orally
transmitted stories that were eventually codified in the form of the Iliad and
the Odyssey.

Be that as it may, the Iliad and the Odyssey are the oldest works of Western
literature and, according to AI, are generally considered to be the
“foundational texts of Western literature and consciousness” and even to
constitute the “bedrock” of Greek culture and Western Civilization in general.
This twin opus fits perfectly in the paradigm of the “Greek Miracle,” the
“Eurocentric” theory, produced by European scholars in the 19th-century, that
the civilization of Ancient Greece, the primordial Western Civilization, had
originated virtually _ex nihilo_ or, to use a Greek expression, had “sprang
fully grown from the brow of Zeus,” like the goddess of wisdom, Athena.

In contrast, many if not most historians now recognize the enormous influence
exerted on Greece by the ancient Mesopotamian Civilization, which originated
in Sumer as early as the 5th millennium BCE but reached its zenith at the time
of the rule of King Hammurabi (1792–1750 BCE), when the region’s metropolis
was Babylon, whose architectural emblem, a ziggurat or step-pyramid with
gardens on its terraces, the so-called “hanging gardens”, was to be declared
by the Greeks themselves to be one of the Seven Wonders of the World. In that
golden age of Mesopotamia, the leading language was no longer Sumerian but
Akkadian.[[2]]() In any event, the notion that the “light” of civilization had
reached Western lands, including Greece, from the east, has been encapsulated
in the aphorism, inspired by the sunrise, _Ex Oriente Lux_ , “the light comes
from the East.”

The “eastern” culture of Mesopotamia came to the “western” Greek world by sea,
via Phoenicia, as well as by land, via Assyria, situated on the upper reaches
of the Tigris River, and the vast highlands of the Anatolian Peninsula. A
similar fecundation of Greece was triggered by impulses originating from
Egypt, again with the Phoenicians functioning as intermediaries, and to a
lesser extent from the Minoan Civilization on Crete, which was not Greek in
the linguistic or cultural sense. It was in those historic circumstances that
Greece’s Mycenaean bronze-age civilization, whose heartland was the
Peloponnese Peninsula, arose in the middle of the second millennium BCE. Homer
did not describe the warriors fighting the historic Trojan War as Greeks: that
appellation did not yet exist in his time.[[3]]() He referred to them by the
name of specific “tribes”, primarily the Achaeans and Danaans (or Danaoi), who
are considered to belong to the ethnicities collectively described as
Mycenaeans.[[4]]() It is also not a coincidence that in the _Iliad_ the Greek
commander, Agamemnon, was the king of Mycenae, a Peloponnesian city whose
impressive ruins constitute one of modern Greece’s major tourist magnets
today, more than 3,000 years after its Mycenaean heyday.

The transfer of Mesopotamian culture to Greece was multidimensional, and it
also featured a very important linguistic component. Akkadian, an Afro-Asiatic
language of the Semitic (as opposed to Hamitic) variety, exerted a
considerable influence on Greek, a member of the Indo-European family (or
“phylum”) of languages, especially on the lexical level. Also important in
this respect was the language of the Phoenicians, who transmitted much
Mesopotamian as well as Egyptian culture to Greece; their idiom also belonged
to the Semitic branch of the Afro-Asiatic family; it was very similar to
Hebrew and, like Hebrew, a close relative of Akkadian.

Ionian Greece, situated on the Aegean Sea at the western extremity of
Anatolia, may be said to have been the hallway through which Mesopotamian as
well as Egyptian cultural and linguistic influence entered the Greek world, to
be diffused from there to the Greek mainland. Already in Antiquity, Ionia was
associated with Homer, who was believed to have lived in Smyrna, or perhaps on
the offshore island of Chios. And according to AI, the Iliad and the Odyssey
were composed in “Homeric Greek,” also known as “Epic Greek” and defined as “a
literary mixture of Ionic Greek and other dialects.” Consequently, it is not
surprising to learn that the Iliad and the Odyssey are teeming with names that
are almost certainly of Akkadian origin.

The name of Homer himself, for example, is almost certainly a form of the
Akkadian term _zammeru_ , which means “singer” or “bard,” as the Italian
paleolinguist Giovanni Semerano (1913–2005), an expert in Mesopotamian
languages, has argued.[[5]]() This interpretation is convincing in light of
the already mentioned fact that the Iliad and the Odyssey were very likely the
fruit of an oral tradition, to be credited to one or more anonymous bards who
had lived long before the epic was put to paper by “Homer or someone else with
the same name,” as Mark Twain famously quipped. A perusal of Semeraro’s
multiple, extensive as well as very thorough studies, especially his two-
volume magnum opus _,__Le origini della cultura Europea_ , published in
Florence in 1984 and 1994, yields countless other examples of Greek words in
general, and names in particular, that appear to have an Akkadian or other
Afro-Asiatic origin; and that includes lots of names associated with Homer,
his world, and his epic poems. Let us examine some of them.

Homer presumably hailed from Ionian Greece, but what does “Ionia” mean? The
name was of Afro-Asiatic origin: it was _Jawan_ in Ancient Egyptian, _Javan_
in Hebrew, and _uwanu_ (or _ummanu_) in Akkadian, and it slipped into the
Indo-European languages of India and Iran as _yavana_ and _yauna_ ; its
meaning was “crowd,” “people,” “humans.” Originally, the name seems to have
had a rather pejorative connotation. The Mesopotamians used it to refer to the
(from their viewpoint) culturally less advanced denizens of Anatolia in
general, regardless of ethnicity or language; but the meaning gradually
shifted to specifically designate the Greeks living along Anatolia’s Aegean
coast and eventually all Greeks, wherever they lived. This explains why even
the waters that stretch from the west coast of the Greek mainland to Italy are
called the “Ionian” Sea, meaning the “Greek” Sea. However, it was the Greeks
living in Anatolia who were commonly referred to as the Ionian Greeks and
their Western Anatolian territory as Ionia. Greeks continued to live there
until their expulsion in the 1920s in the wake of a war between Greece and
Turkey. As for the Turks, when they migrated into the Middle East and all the
way to Anatolia from their Central Asian homeland around 1,000 CE, they
adopted a variant of the ancient Iranian appellation for Greece, and even
today, they call Greece Yunanistan, “land [_stan_] of the Ionians.”[[6]]()

It was likely in Ionia that the Greeks borrowed an Akkadian term to designate
the lands to the west, on the far side of the Aegean Sea, namely _ereb(u)_ ,
which meant “[land of] the setting sun”, “sunset”, “evening”, and turned it
into “Europe”.[[7]]() In German and in Dutch, synonyms for Europe are
_Abendland_ and _Avondland,_ respectively, meaning“land of the evening”: a
perfect interpretation of _ereb!_

But let us focus on the theme of Homer and his famous epic poems about the
Trojan War and its aftermath. The title Iliad refers to Ilion or Ilium which,
as already mentioned, was another name used by the Greeks to designate Troy.
Ilion is a toponym of Mesopotamian origin, it conjures up the Akkadian noun
_ilum_ or _elum_ , meaning “upper part of a city,” “citadel.” As for the name
Troy, it reflects the Akkadian verb _tarum_ , “to circle [with a wall],” and
therefore signifies “walled city.”[[8]]() Both names essentially designated a
fortified city on a hill, which corresponds to the topography of Troy.

Odysseus was one of the great heroes of the Trojan War, on the Greek side,
that is. He was the brain behind the famous equine subterfuge that sealed the
Greeks’ victory, and he was of course the protagonist of Homer’s second opus,
which was even named after him, the Odyssey. He personified the intelligence,
bravery, and personal integrity ascribed to the Greeks but, like Homer, he
actually has a Mesopotamian pedigree. Why else would he have a name that
cannot be interpreted with the help of the Greek language but can easily be
deconstructed with a little knowledge of Akkadian? The first part of the
hero’s name conjures up no less than a duo of terms from that Babylonian
idiom, _(w)udu_ , “wise person,” and _edu_ or _idu_ , “to be experienced”, “to
know”, etc.; and the second part of his name echoes _ussu_ , Akkadian for
“guide” or “leader.”[[9]]() That combination proclaims Odysseus to be a “wise
leader”, wise, that is, from experiences in war and especially in travel. A
plausible interpretation, is it not, particularly since in Homer’s epos as
well as in the movie by Christopher Nolan, the hero’s wisdom is largely the
fruit of his experiences during a long voyage?

In this context it is worth pointing out that Gilgamesh, the protagonist of a
famous Mesopotamian epic story, who is often cited as a prototype for Homeric
and other Greek heroes, likewise achieved great wisdom in the course of a long
and perilous journey.[[10]]() For comparison purposes, the story of Gilgamesh
dates back to about 2,000 BCE, so it was already more than 1,000 years old
when the Iliad and the Odyssey were put on papyrus! Odysseus, the traveler,
was also known in Greek as Oulixeus, which produced Ulixes in Latin, Ulysse in
French and Ulysses in English; that term conjures up the Akkadian verb
_alik(su)_ , which signified… “to move about,” “to travel.”[[11]]()

As for Odysseus’ wife, her name, Penelope, can also be interpreted as an echo
of Akkadian terms. Semerano argues that the name would originally have started
not with pene- but with kene-, and that kene- corresponds to the Akkadian
_kenu,_ meaning “true, faithful feelings”. The Italian paleolinguist
interprets the name’s second part as a form of the Akkadian _libbu,_ “heart”
or “sentiment.”[[12]]() Penelope thus comes to mean “faithful heart.” It is an
appellation she richly deserved, waiting faithfully for a decade for her
warrior husband to return home.

In the movie, but not in Homer’s story, Penelope finds herself under pressure
to marry so that Ithaca may be more effectively defended by a male leader
against a potential attack by shadowy foreign marauders known as the Sea
Peoples. This is a subplot invented by Christopher Nolan and its purpose is
revealed at the end of the movie. Nolan was inspired by the historic fact that
the end of the Bronze Age featured violent incursions into that era’s leading
empires by hitherto unknown but very warlike folks from distant overseas
lands, referred to as the “Sea Peoples.” These marauders were expelled from
Egypt by Pharaoh Rames III, though not without difficulty, but they are
believed to be responsible for the collapse of the Anatolia-based empire of
the Hittites.

What about Telemachus, the brave son of Odysseus and Penelope? AI would have
us believe that the name “combines [the Greek term] _tele_ , meaning ‘far off’
. . ., and _makhe_ , meaning ‘battle’ or ‘fight,’…which translates to ‘far-
fighter,’ or ‘distant warrior,’ whatever that may mean. Semerano, on the other
hand, while not referring to Telemachus by name, provides clues for a
different and more convincing interpretation. Both parts of the name
Telemachus appear to be derived from the Akkadian language. The first one
reflects the term _tele’u_ , meaning “competent” and “brave”, which Semerano
claims to recognize in the name of the mythological hero Telephus, a son of
Heracles (Hercules); and the second part is a form of the verb _mahasu_ , “to
fight” or “to kill,” a verb from which the Greek term _makhe_ was derived.
Telemachus did indeed prove to be an efficient fighter/killer, assisting his
father in the massacre of his mother’s suitors [[13]]()

content/uploads/2026/08/telemachusslaughter-680x537.png)

Odysseus and Telemachus slaughter the suitors of Penelope on a painting by
Thomas Degeorge.

Let us accompany Odysseus to some of the intriguing places he visited during
his long and adventurous journey throughout the Mediterranean. The hero was
held captive for many years by the nymph Calypso, whose name is known to
reflect an Ancient Greek verb _kalypto_ , meaning “to conceal” or “to hide”,
making her “she who hides [in a cave].” What is less known, however, is that
this Greek verb was nothing other than a variant of the Akkadian _halapu_ ,
with the same meaning.[[14]]()

As for the sirens, whose seductive but fatal songs Odysseus was eager to hear
but could only hold out against because his men had tied him to the mast of
his ship, their name can likewise be deconstructed and interpreted with the
help of the Afro-Asiatic language of Babylon and Mesopotamia in general. The
word “siren” appears to be a combination of the root _sur_ , “rocks”, and
_(w)enu_ , “source”, “river”, “water,” and alludes to rocks lurking just below
or above the water surface, a grave threat to inattentive sailors; in
addition, the first part of “siren” conjures up two Afro-Asiatic terms, the
Sumerian _sir_ and the Aramaic _sar,_ respectively meaning ‘song” and “to
sing.” The story of the sirens has often been associated with the Italian town
of Sorrento and the homonymous peninsula, separated from the island of Capri
by a narrow strait of tumultuous and dangerous waters that also feature two
rocky islets responsible in the past for numerous shipwrecks; now called the
Galli, they were known in the past as the _Sirene_ , Italian for
“Sirens.”[[15]]()

The toponym Sorrento – _Surrentum_ in Latin – clearly also contains the term
_sur,_ “rock,” which simultaneously conjures up another Akkadian word, _saru,_
“high”; and the name also seems to hide the Akkadian word for “water,”
_(w)enu._ As for the final syllable of Sorrento, it is likely a variant of an
Afro-Asiatic term designating a land or locality, _ta_ in Ancient Egyptian and
_etu_ in Semitic idioms such as Akkadian.[[16]]() This produces the very
plausible meaning of “town on the high rocks overlooking the water,” it
happens to be a perfectly accurate description of Sorrento’s picturesque site
on top of lofty cliffs rising perpendicularly from the blue waters of the Bay
of Naples.

En route to Sorrento to hear the Siren songs, Odysseus and his band of
brothers slipped through the Strait of Messina, which separates the tip of the
Italian boot from the island of Sicily; this narrow stretch of water features
cliffs and rocks as well as dangerous currents, including whirlpools,
undertows, and such, and is believed to have provided the inspiration for the
story of the terrifying monsters Scylla and Charibdys. In Nolan’s film,
Odysseus narrowly avoids being swallowed _in toto_ by a gaping vortex, but a
good number of his men are subsequently snatched and devoured by a cliff-
dwelling monster. The vortex is the monster Charybdis and the terrifying
creature with multiple necks and heads is Scylla, and their names reflect
Akkadian terminology: the former conjures up _haribtu_ , “womb” or “uterus”,
and the latter, _kullu_ , “to snatch.”[[17]]()

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/odysseus3.png)

Odysseus passes Scylla and Charybdis and is tied to the mast of his ship while
sailing by the Sirens on a lithograph by Theodoor van Thulden, Paris, 1633.

Odysseus returned from his decade-long voyage “full of experience and wisdom”
(_plein d 'usage et raison_), as a French poet of the Renaissance, Joachim du
Bellay, wrote in a beautiful poem quoted earlier and as Christopher Nolan
emphasizes in his own cinematographic way towards the end of his production.
That is when the hero shares with Penelope something he had come to understand
during his long and arduous homeward voyage, namely that the Greeks’ triumph
over Troy, made possible by his ruse with the horse, had not been a glorious
affair but a terrible massacre, a feat warranting not pride, but remorse. The
Greeks, he confides to Penelope, were in fact the Sea Peoples, or a host
similar to the Sea Peoples, the shadowy marauders who had struck fear in the
hearts of the denizens of Ithaca, a fear that triggered pressure on her to
marry one of the suitors. The writer-director makes his point
cinematographically by having the Trojan Horse dragged into Troy directly from
the sea.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-19-at-3.10.53-PM-680x353.png)

Sea Peoples fighting Egyptians on a wall of the temple of Ramses III in
Medinet Habu near Luxor, Egypt.

Nolan’s notion that the Greeks besieging and destroying Troy were part of the
infamous Sea Peoples is far from outlandish. Homer’s epic was inspired by a
real war, fought around 1,200 BC, exactly at the time of the traumatic end of
the Bronze Age, when “peoples from the sea” raided Egypt and ruined the empire
of the Hittites based in Anatolia. Egyptian records contain lists with names
of ethnicities belonging to that infamous horde, and they include Bronze-Age
Greeks such as the Achaeans of the Iliad and the Odyssey, who are also
believed to be the _Ahhiyawa_ mentioned in contemporary Hittite texts.[[18]]()
And many historians equate Troy with Wilusa, a city in northwestern Anatolia
that was part of, or perhaps a satellite, of the Hittite Empire.[[19]]() These
data do not prove, but certainly suggest, that the Trojan War may have been an
operation carried out by Mycenaean Greeks within the general context of the
destruction, by marauders from overseas, of the once-mighty state of the
Hittites

According to an ancient proverb, those who “live by the sword,” will also “die
by the sword,” and this is what eventually happened to the Mycenaean Greeks.
Their civilization, like that of the Hittites, also collapsed in the twilight
of the Bronze Age, and its demise is certain to have involved armed conflict,
although it is not clear with whom. The Mycenaeans left behind impressive
ruins that were also excavated by Schliemann and yielded treasures such as a
wonderful golden mask the German antiquarian wrongly believed to represent
Agamemnon, the Greek commander who, in the movie, is dressed in a jet-black
suit of armor and looks like Darth Vader; described as the “Mona Lisa of
prehistory,” the mask is now on display in the National Archaeological Museum
of Athens.

As for Odysseus, no golden mask seems to exist, even though he was
indisputably not only a great hero like Agamemnon, Achilles, etc., but also a
decent and smart “good guy,” the “golden boy” of Homer’s opus. Maybe he was
not considered to be sufficiently Greek to be receive such a high honor?
Indeed, as we have seen, for his post-war adventures, Homer had him sailing
off to western lands before finally returning to his island on the west coast
of Greece, but the cunning hero’s origins were in the east: _Ex Oriente
Odysseus!_

_Jacques Pauwels is the author of_[Beneath the Dust of Time: A History of
Ancient Languages and Names of Peoples and
Places,](https://www.jacquespauwels.net/books/beneath-the-dust-of-time-a-
history-of-the-names-of-peoples-and-places-2025-edition/)_published in 2025 by
Trine Day in Walterville/OR, a book that deals with topics such as the
influence of the Akkadian language of Babylon and other Afro-Asiatic languages
on the Greek language and culture in general._
